questions.question: According to the context, why does logic reasoning not apply well to learned knowledge?

options.A: Because learned knowledge is often expressed in first‑order logic already
options.B: Because learned knowledge is hardly deterministic, conflicting with logic reasoning’s requirement for discrete, deterministic KBs
options.C: Because logic reasoning cannot handle any form of inference
options.D: Because learned knowledge always includes visual information

questions.explanation:
The text notes that “learned knowledge is hardly deterministic (it cannot be in a Bayesian view), logic reasoning does not really apply well” [Page 199].

---

questions.question: Which issue is identified as a core problem with GOFAI in the provided material?

options.A: Its inability to represent objects and relations
options.B: Its reliance on probabilistic graphical models
options.C: The fact that logic reasoning does not unify well with learning and learned models

questions.explanation:
The passage states that “one of the core problems with GOFAI: the fact that logic reasoning does not unify well with learning and learned models” [Page 199].

---

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why first‑order (relational) representations are advocated for strong generalization?

options.A: They encode the exact identities of objects to avoid ambiguity
options.B: They represent knowledge solely through object properties and relations, allowing generalization across object identities
options.C: They eliminate the need for any inference procedures
options.D: They guarantee deterministic outcomes for all queries

questions.explanation:
The context says that first‑order representations “refer only to object properties and relations, and therefore generalize across object identities” and are needed “for strong generalization” [Page 199, 222].

---

questions.question: Based on the description of probabilistic relational approaches, what is a direct implication of making predictions only from properties/relations and not object identity?

options.A: The approach cannot handle uncertainty in the data
options.B: It enables knowledge learned in one world to be applied to a different world with new objects
options.C: It requires the explicit enumeration of all possible object identities
options.D: It restricts the model to deterministic inference only

questions.explanation:
The material notes that such approaches “make predictions based only on the properties/relations of objects, not their identity” and “generalize data seen in one world … to another world” [Page 222].

---

questions.question: What limitation of classical first‑order knowledge bases (FOL) concerning uncertain knowledge is highlighted in the text?

options.A: They are inherently probabilistic and thus too vague for precise reasoning
options.B: They are deterministic, making it difficult to represent uncertain or learned knowledge
options.C: They cannot express any object properties or relations
options.D: They automatically integrate Bayesian learning without extra effort

questions.explanation: The passage points out that “logic reasoning … is only applicable on discrete & deterministic knowledge bases” and that “learned knowledge is hardly deterministic,” indicating a limitation of classical FOL for uncertainty [Page 199].
